name: Few TensoRF

# Few TensoRF
## Overview
Few TensoRF is a 3D reconstruction framework that combines the efficient tensor-based representation of [TensoRF](3026-tensorf.md) with [frequency-driven regularization](#6130-frequency-regularization.md) from [FreeNeRF](3027-freenerf.md) to improve stability and reconstruction quality under sparse input views [S1, unofficial]. It addresses the problem of high-frequency artifacts and bias that occur when TensoRF converges too rapidly on high-frequency components during few-shot training [S1, unofficial]. By applying a dynamic frequency mask to tensor components, Few TensoRF forces the model to prioritize low-frequency information in early training stages, enhancing data efficiency without sacrificing the fast training times characteristic of the parent method [S1, unofficial].

## How it works
**Inputs and Outputs:**
Inputs consist of a sparse set of images, camera poses, and intrinsics [G]. Outputs are the factorized radiance field grids and rendered novel views [S1, unofficial].

**Data Structures:**
The radiance field is modeled using two distinct grids employing [Vector-Matrix (VM) decomposition](#3452-vector-matrix-vm-decomposition.md): a geometry grid $G_\sigma$ for density $\sigma$ and an appearance grid $G_c$ for features [S1, unofficial]. Density and features are derived via trilinear interpolation at location $x$ as $\sigma(x) = G_\sigma(x)$ and $\mathbf{c}_{feat}(x) = G_c(x)$ [S1, unofficial]. Final color is computed as $c = S(\mathbf{c}_{feat}(x), \mathbf{d})$, where $\mathbf{d}$ is the viewing direction and $S$ is a pre-selected function like a small MLP or [spherical harmonics](#5603-spherical-harmonics.md) [S1, unofficial].

**Tensor [Decomposition](#7254-decomposition.md):**
The appearance grid decomposes as $G_c(x) = \sum_{r=1}^{R_o} (A^X_{c,r} \circ b^{3r-2} + A^Y_{c,r} \circ b^{3r-2} + A^Z_{c,r} \circ b^{3r})$, where $R_o$ is rank, $r$ is the index, $A$ are tensor components, $b$ are basis vectors, and $\circ$ is the combination operation [S1, unofficial]. The density grid $G_\sigma$ follows a similar VM structure [S1, unofficial].

**Frequency Masking:**
To mitigate over-fast convergence in high-frequency components, a dynamic frequency mask $\alpha(t, T, L)$ is applied to density components $A$ and appearance components $A_c$ [S1, unofficial]. The masked component is $A'_L(t, T; x) = A_L(x) \odot \alpha(t, T, L)$, where $\odot$ is element-wise multiplication [S1, unofficial]. The mask value for the $i$-th bit is $\alpha_i(t, T, L) = \begin{cases} 1 & \text{if } i \le \frac{t \cdot L}{T} \\ \frac{t \cdot L}{T} - \lfloor \frac{t \cdot L}{T} \rfloor & \text{if } \frac{t \cdot L}{T} < i \le \frac{t \cdot L}{T} + 6 \\ 0 & \text{if } i > \frac{t \cdot L}{T} + 6 \end{cases}$ [S1, unofficial]. Here $t$ is the current iteration, $T$ is total iterations, and $L$ is the component length [S1, unofficial]. If $t \ge T$, the mask returns a tensor of ones [S1, unofficial].

**Algorithm Steps:**
1. Initialize $G_\sigma$ and $G_c$ with VM decomposition factors [G].
2. For each training iteration $t$ from 1 to $T$:
   a. Sample rays and compute $\sigma(x)$ and $\mathbf{c}_{feat}(x)$ via trilinear interpolation from the grids [S1, unofficial].
   b. Compute $\alpha(t, T, L)$ for both density and appearance components based on $t$ and $T$ [S1, unofficial].
   c. Apply the mask to tensor factors $A$ and $A_c$ using element-wise multiplication [S1, unofficial].
   d. Render the [image using volume rendering](#11273-image-based-volume-rendering.md) integration [G].
   e. Compute loss against ground truth images [G].
   f. Backpropagate and update the tensor factors [G].
3. After training, render novel views using the final factors [S1, unofficial].

**Parameters:**
$T$ is the total training iterations, aligning with approximately 10–15 minutes of optimization [S1, unofficial]. $L$ is the length of the tensor component being masked [S1, unofficial]. $S$ is the color prediction function (MLP or SH) [S1, unofficial].

**Edge Cases and Pitfalls:**
Rapid convergence in high-frequency components hinders the exploration of low-frequency information, causing bias and undesired high-frequency artifacts in sparse scenarios [S1, unofficial].

## Operating characteristics
Time complexity maintains the fast training time of TensoRF, approximately 10–15 minutes [S1, unofficial]. Memory complexity inherits the low memory footprint of the VM decomposition from [TensoRF](3026-tensorf.md) [G]. On the Synthesis [NeRF](#1185-nerf-neural-radiance-fields.md) benchmark, Few TensoRF improves average PSNR from 21.45 dB (standard TensoRF) to 23.70 dB, with a fine-tuned version reaching 24.52 dB [S1, unofficial]. On the THuman 2.0 dataset, it achieves 27.37–34.00 dB PSNR with only eight input images [S1, unofficial]. Strengths include high data efficiency for few-shot inputs, prevention of high-frequency artifacts, and retention of real-time rendering speed [S1, unofficial]. Limitations include reliance on the frequency mask schedule and performance tied to the specific few-shot regime [S1, unofficial].

## Background
Few TensoRF was introduced by authors from FPT University, Ho Chi Minh City, Vietnam, in a paper published in March 2026 [S1, unofficial]. It builds directly on [TensoRF](3026-tensorf.md) and incorporates [regularization techniques](#11314-regularization-techniques.md) from [FreeNeRF](3027-freenerf.md) to address the limitations of tensor-based radiance fields in sparse view settings [S1, unofficial].

## Sources
